title: Case Study: Food Delivery (Zomato/Swiggy)
summary: Design a food-delivery platform end to end — the order-lifecycle state machine and delivery-agent assignment are the parts that separate a working design from a broken one.

blocks.markdown:
**Design a food-delivery platform** like Zomato or Swiggy: customers browse restaurants, build a cart from a menu, place an order, the system assigns a delivery agent, and everyone tracks status until the food arrives.

- The hard part isn't CRUD — it's the **order lifecycle** (a strict state machine) and **agent assignment** under live, changing agent locations.
- Draws on the same toolkit as [case-study-parking-lot](case-study-parking-lot): entities, patterns, then the one decision that makes or breaks the design.
- Use [lld-interview-framework](lld-interview-framework) as the general approach; this topic is that framework applied to a marketplace with three actors instead of one.

blocks.subTitle: Functional
blocks.markdown:
What the system must do:

- **Browse restaurants** near the customer and view each one's **menu**.
- **Cart**: add/remove menu items, see a running total before checkout.
- **Place an order** against a restaurant, referencing the cart's items.
- **Assign a delivery agent** to a placed order automatically.
- **Track order status** in real time (placed → delivered).
- **Payment** at checkout, and a **rating** for the restaurant and agent after delivery.

blocks.subTitle: Non-functional
blocks.markdown:
What the system must guarantee, not just do:

- **Consistency of order state** — an order can never skip states or go backwards (no jumping from Placed to Delivered).
- **Low-latency assignment** — picking a delivery agent must happen in near real time, not via a batch job.
- **Real-time visibility** — customer, restaurant, and agent all need the current status without polling a slow query.
- **Extensibility** — new payment methods or a smarter assignment algorithm should slot in without touching order logic.

**Noun extraction** on the requirements gives the entity list; verbs that don't belong on a data class become **strategies**.

| Noun in requirements | Becomes |
|---|---|
| customer, cart | `Customer`, `Cart` |
| restaurant, menu, dish | `Restaurant`, `Menu`, `MenuItem` |
| order, status | `Order`, `OrderStatus` |
| delivery agent | `DeliveryAgent` |

"Assigns the nearest agent" and "finds restaurants" are behaviors, not fields — they become `AgentAssignmentStrategy` and a search service.

blocks.subTitle: Customer & Cart
blocks.markdown:
A customer owns exactly one active cart at a time; the cart accumulates items before becoming an order.

```text
class Customer:
    id: String
    name: String
    address: Address
    cart: Cart
    orderHistory: List<Order>

class CartItem:
    menuItem: MenuItem
    quantity: int

class Cart:
    restaurantId: String        // all items must come from one restaurant
    items: List<CartItem>

    method addItem(menuItem: MenuItem, qty: int):
        if items.isNotEmpty() and menuItem.restaurantId != restaurantId:
            throw MixedRestaurantException()
        items.add(new CartItem(menuItem, qty))

    method total(): Money:
        return items.sum(i -> i.menuItem.price * i.quantity)

    method clear():
        items = []
```

blocks.subTitle: Restaurant, Menu & MenuItem
blocks.markdown:
A restaurant composes one menu; a menu composes items. Availability lives on the item, not scattered elsewhere.

```text
class MenuItem:
    id: String
    restaurantId: String
    name: String
    price: Money
    isAvailable: boolean = true

class Menu:
    items: List<MenuItem>

    method availableItems(): List<MenuItem>:
        return items.filter(i -> i.isAvailable)

class Restaurant:
    id: String
    name: String
    location: GeoPoint
    menu: Menu
    isOpen: boolean = true
    rating: float

    method canServe(item: MenuItem): boolean:
        return isOpen and item.isAvailable
```

blocks.subTitle: Order & OrderStatus
blocks.markdown:
The order is the record of truth for a transaction — it snapshots cart items so later menu price changes never alter a past order.

```text
enum OrderStatusType:
    PLACED
    ACCEPTED
    PREPARING
    OUT_FOR_DELIVERY
    DELIVERED
    CANCELLED

class Order:
    id: String
    customer: Customer
    restaurant: Restaurant
    items: List<CartItem>          // snapshot, not a live cart reference
    status: OrderState             // see State pattern card
    agent: DeliveryAgent = null
    payment: Payment
    placedAt: DateTime

    method total(): Money:
        return items.sum(i -> i.menuItem.price * i.quantity)
```

blocks.subTitle: OrderState — the lifecycle as a State machine
blocks.markdown:
The lifecycle is the crux of this design. Instead of one big `if status == X` chain, each status is a class that knows only its own legal next transitions.

```text
interface OrderState:
    method next(order: Order): OrderState
    method name(): OrderStatusType

class PlacedState implements OrderState:
    method next(order): OrderState:
        order.notifyRestaurant()
        return new AcceptedState()
    method name(): return OrderStatusType.PLACED

class AcceptedState implements OrderState:
    method next(order): OrderState:
        return new PreparingState()
    method name(): return OrderStatusType.ACCEPTED

class PreparingState implements OrderState:
    method next(order): OrderState:
        agent = order.assignmentStrategy.assignAgent(order)
        order.agent = agent
        return new OutForDeliveryState()
    method name(): return OrderStatusType.PREPARING

class OutForDeliveryState implements OrderState:
    method next(order): OrderState:
        order.agent.markAvailable()
        return new DeliveredState()
    method name(): return OrderStatusType.OUT_FOR_DELIVERY

class DeliveredState implements OrderState:
    method next(order): OrderState:
        throw IllegalTransitionException()   // terminal state
    method name(): return OrderStatusType.DELIVERED
```

Calling `order.status.next(order)` is the only way status ever changes — an illegal jump (Placed straight to Delivered) simply has no method that produces it.

blocks.subTitle: DeliveryAgent
blocks.markdown:
An agent's location and availability change constantly — both live directly on the agent so assignment always reads live state.

```text
class DeliveryAgent:
    id: String
    name: String
    currentLocation: GeoPoint
    isAvailable: boolean = true
    activeOrderCount: int = 0

    method markBusy():
        isAvailable = false
        activeOrderCount += 1

    method markAvailable():
        activeOrderCount = max(0, activeOrderCount - 1)
        isAvailable = activeOrderCount == 0

    method updateLocation(point: GeoPoint):
        currentLocation = point   // pushed by the agent's app every few seconds
```

blocks.subTitle: AgentAssignmentStrategy — nearest vs least-busy
Payment
blocks.markdown:
Payment methods multiply fast (card, wallet, UPI, cash-on-delivery) — a **Factory** keeps that variation out of `Order`.

```text
interface PaymentMethod:
    method pay(amount: Money): PaymentResult

class CardPayment implements PaymentMethod:
    method pay(amount): PaymentResult: return gateway.charge(amount)

class WalletPayment implements PaymentMethod:
    method pay(amount): PaymentResult: return wallet.debit(amount)

class CashOnDelivery implements PaymentMethod:
    method pay(amount): PaymentResult: return PaymentResult.pending()

class PaymentFactory:
    static method create(kind: String): PaymentMethod:
        switch kind:
            case "card": return new CardPayment()
            case "wallet": return new WalletPayment()
            case "cod": return new CashOnDelivery()

class Payment:
    order: Order
    method: PaymentMethod
    amount: Money
    status: String

    method process():
        result = method.pay(amount)
        status = result.status
```

blocks.subTitle: Restaurant search & OrderService
blocks.markdown:
Search is its own strategy too — "nearby" today, "nearby and highly rated" tomorrow, without rewriting the browse screen. `OrderService` is the façade that ties everything together.

```text
interface RestaurantSearchStrategy:
    method search(location: GeoPoint, query: String): List<Restaurant>

class NearbySearchStrategy implements RestaurantSearchStrategy:
    method search(location, query): List<Restaurant>:
        return restaurants
            .filter(r -> distance(r.location, location) <= MAX_RADIUS_KM)
            .filter(r -> query == null or r.name.matches(query))
            .sortedBy(r -> distance(r.location, location))

class OrderService:
    searchStrategy: RestaurantSearchStrategy
    assignmentStrategy: AgentAssignmentStrategy

    method placeOrder(customer: Customer): Order:
        order = new Order(customer, customer.cart.restaurantId, customer.cart.items)
        order.status = new PlacedState()
        customer.cart.clear()
        notifyObservers(order)          // see Observer card
        return order

    method advance(order: Order):
        order.status = order.status.next(order)
        notifyObservers(order)
```

Where each pattern earns its place in this design:

| Pattern | Where it's used |
|---|---|
| State | `OrderState` — legal transitions only, no status if-chain |
| Strategy | `AgentAssignmentStrategy` (nearest/least-busy) and search |
| Observer | Order tracking — customer, restaurant, agent all get pushed updates |
| Factory | `PaymentFactory` builds a `PaymentMethod` from a type string |

Each replaces logic that would otherwise be duplicated or hardcoded inside `Order` or `OrderService`. See [behavioral-patterns-i](behavioral-patterns-i) for State, Strategy, and Observer in general form.

Three parties — customer, restaurant, agent — must all see status changes the instant they happen, without polling.

- `Order` (or `OrderService`) is the **subject**; the customer's app, restaurant's dashboard, and agent's app each register as **observers**.
- Every `advance()` call fires a notification carrying the new `OrderStatus` to all three, typically over a push channel (WebSocket) rather than the observers polling a REST endpoint.
- This decouples `OrderService` from *how* each party is notified — adding an SMS notifier later means adding one more observer, not touching order logic.

How the design absorbs real follow-up requirements without a rewrite:

- **Order cancellation** — add a `CancelledState` reachable from `Placed`/`Accepted` only; `PreparingState` onward rejects it, keeping the "no illegal transition" guarantee intact.
- **Group orders / split payment** — `Payment` already isolates the charge step, so splitting one order's total across multiple `PaymentMethod` calls doesn't touch `Order` or `OrderState`.
- **Trade-off**: a full state-class hierarchy is heavier than an enum for a lifecycle this short — worth it here because illegal transitions are a real production bug class, not a hypothetical.

blocks.subTitle: Modeling the order lifecycle
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you model the order lifecycle so illegal transitions are impossible?**

Use the **State** pattern instead of a status enum plus `if` chains. Each status (Placed, Accepted, Preparing, OutForDelivery, Delivered) is its own class implementing `next()`, and that method is the *only* place a transition is produced. A state simply has no method that jumps to a non-adjacent status, so the illegal case can't be expressed rather than being caught by a runtime check.

blocks.subTitle: Assigning a delivery agent
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you assign a delivery agent to an order?**

Pull assignment out into an `AgentAssignmentStrategy` interface with implementations like nearest-agent (minimize pickup distance) or least-busy (balance load). The strategy queries only agents with `isAvailable = true` and picks by its own metric. Keeping it a strategy means swapping in a smarter scoring model later doesn't touch `Order` or `OrderService`.

blocks.subTitle: Which patterns fit
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Which design patterns fit a food-delivery platform, and why?**

State for the order lifecycle, since transitions must be constrained and one-directional. Strategy for both agent assignment and restaurant search, since each policy changes independently of the core order flow. Observer for real-time tracking, since three different parties need push updates. Factory for payment methods, since new payment types shouldn't require editing `Order`.

blocks.subTitle: Tracking order status in real time
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How do you track order status in real time across customer, restaurant, and agent apps?**

Make `OrderService` (or `Order` itself) a subject in the **Observer** pattern; each app registers as an observer when it opens the order screen. On every state transition, push the new status to all registered observers over a persistent channel like WebSocket, instead of having each client poll a status endpoint every few seconds.

blocks.subTitle: Handling restaurant search
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How would you handle restaurant search at scale?**

Behind a `RestaurantSearchStrategy` interface, start with a simple radius filter plus sort-by-distance. At real scale, the naive linear scan is replaced by a **geospatial index** (geohash or quad-tree) so "restaurants within 5km" is an index lookup, not a full table scan — the strategy interface means that swap never touches the browse screen's calling code.

blocks.subTitle: Why not one Order class with a status flag
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why not just keep a `status` string on `Order` and branch on it everywhere?**

It works briefly, but every new status or rule means finding and updating every branch that checks it — a violation of the **open/closed principle**, and a common source of the "order silently skipped a state" bug class. The State pattern confines each transition's logic to one class, so adding `CancelledState` later touches one new file instead of every call site that reads `order.status`.
